utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Good morning. The Bench apologises to you for the few minutes of lateness. We were engaged -- the colleagues were engaged in another matter, but now we're ready to go. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-98-30/1-A, the Prosecutor versus Miroslav Kvocka, Mladjo Radic, Zoran Zigic, and Dragoljub Prcac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: This hearing is continuing this morning with the taking of the evidence of Witness KV4, so let me inquire if everyone can hear me in the courtroom, and I think also elsewhere as well? Mr. Re, would you have any objection to the name of the country from which the video is being transmitted being mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Certainly not in closed session, as everyone in the courtroom is aware of it, but in open session this witness has particular concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Okay. Well now, can the interpreters hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The appellants? And the Defence counsel? And the counsel for the Prosecutor? Yes. Yes. Well, thank you very much. The appearances are as before. I would like to make a few brief introductory remarks before we proceed with the evidentiary phase of this appeal hearing. We have heard yesterday Witness KV3, who was an additional witness admitted on appeal by a decision dated 12 March 2004, the Appeals Chamber found also admissible as rebuttal material the evidence contained in the witness statement submitted by Prosecution Witness KV4. By order dated 2 July 2004, that witness was called to testify in this case as a rebuttal witness. The order dated 2 July 2004 granted certain provisional measures to Witness KV4, who will testify today with voice and facial distortion. So now, can we turn to the other place. Yes. The witness is there before me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, could you please read the solemn declaration given to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, by orders dated 2 July and 14 July 2004, this witness was granted the pseudonym KV4 and will be testifying with voice and face distortion, as I said a while ago. I remind all parties to use this pseudonym at all times during this hearing. Now, Madam Registrar in the place in which the witness is sitting, could you show the witness his name on a sheet of paper and proceed with the usual form for identification of the witness. THE VIDEOLINK REGISTRAR: Can you identify that this is your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is my first and last name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Good. Good. Well, Madam Registrar over there, may I remind you that you are an officer of the court; you are aware of the nature of the proceedings and of the nature of the mission which you have undertaken and of the identity of the witness concerned. So now, may I turn to the registrar here and ask the registrar to do likewise in relation to defence counsel, prosecuting counsel, and the Bench. Thank you, Witness KV4. You are here to testify in the appeal proceedings in the case of the Prosecutor against Miroslav Kvocka and others. The Prosecution will be the first to ask you questions, and you will be cross-examined by counsel for the appellant Mr. Zigic. The other appellants or their counsel may also be asking you questions. The Judges may at any time intervene and certainly will reserve a time when they will en bloc ask you questions if they wish. So, Mr. Counsel for the Prosecution, would you open.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. KV4. Can I ask you first of all whether you can firstly clearly see and hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you well. But I can't really see you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My name is David Re. I'm going to ask you some questions about your time in Omarska for the Prosecution. I'm going to ask you some very general questions at first, very briefly, then take you to a specific incident which is the focus of our attention here today. Firstly, your -- can you please tell the Appeals Chamber your ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: I'm a Bosniak, a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And were you living in the Prijedor region in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And were you arrested on the 31st of May, 1992 by armed Serbs and taken to the Prijedor police station and put on a bus to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Yes. On the 31st of May, 1992 I was taken from in front of my house on foot together with my other neighbours, from my house through the village of Cereke up to the Raskovac neighbourhood --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, they're certainly not. I was just bending down because I'm getting no interpretation on the channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] No, I said that these are not disputed matters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, they're not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. KV2, were you kept --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: KV4. You said "KV2".

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I apologise. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. KV4, when you arrived at Omarska, were you kept with a number of other prisoners on an area called the pista, an outdoor area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Yes. Upon arriving at Omarska, together with the other prisoners, I was on what was known as the pista. It is an asphalted area between two buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And were you kept outside on the pista for the whole -- for a considerable period after you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Yes. After I arrived, I was on the pista for about a month. And before leaving Omarska, for another ten days, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And did you leave Omarska in August 1992? When the camp closed, were you taken to another camp called Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: From Omarska, I was taken on the 3rd of August, 1992. Actually, I left Omarska three days before Omarska started to be dismantled.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In 1992, before you went to Omarska, did you know a person called Becir Medunjanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Yes, I did know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How well did you know him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Actually, I knew his wife better, because we are the same generation. We would meet occasionally in Prijedor, as he lived in the neighbourhood called Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you know his sons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Medunjanin when you were detained at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: I saw him only once, in the so-called "white house."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown a copy of the diagram tendered yesterday, which has a number on appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. KV4, where was the "white house" in relation to the pista?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what you mean. When you reach the pista from Omarska, the "white house" was to the right of the pista.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If you just look at the diagram which is on the ELMO or the colour photo on the ELMO. Do you recognise that as an overhead photograph depicting the rooms inside the building you described as the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: The rooms are marked with "A1" to "A6". Is this the layout of the "white house"? Yes, it is. I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said you saw Mr. Medunjanin only once in the "white house". I want you to tell the Appeals Chamber the circumstances. Where were you before you went into the "white house" and why did you go into the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: As I have already said, we were on the pista. When there is a storm or a heavy rain and wind, in that case the prisoners from the pista were put up in other premises in the camp to protect them from the weather. I think it was around the 20th of June - I'm not sure about Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond that, but round about then - there was a heavy storm, and together with a group of prisoners I was ushered into the "white house" until the storm waned. Entering the "white house," in the room on the left, as the doors were half in glass, I saw Sadeta and Becir as I passed by. I was taken to the next room, which was empty, and all of us who had come from the pista were put inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I just ask you to pause there for one moment. You referred to a room on the left in which you saw Sadeta and Becir. Was Sadeta Mr. Medunjanin's wife?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And if you look at the diagram, was that room, the one on the left, was that A3?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Yes, it is room A3.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said you were taken to the next room; was that A4?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Yes, A4 is next to A3. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And doing your best, about how many people did you see in A3 and then how many people were in A4 with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: In -- I saw A3 only as I passed, and I saw prisoners either lying or sitting against the wall. How many of them there were, I don't know exactly. The room I went to, with me were about 40 prisoners in the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What happened after you were put into room A4 with the 40 other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Two persons in uniform arrived and entered room A3. One could hear some movement in there, and after some time Medunjanin was thrown out into the corridor. I recognised one of the two as Zigic, whom I knew from before the war as a taxi driver in Prijedor, but I didn't know the other man. Other prisoners said that it was someone called Duca. They beat Medunjanin with batons and a cable. They kicked him. At first Medunjanin was lying and moving left and right, and later on he no longer reacted to the blows. His head was covered in blood. This is what I saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Re, could you ask the witness to clarify whom he meant by his reference to "they." Who beat Medunjanin? Who kicked Medunjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I most certainly will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. KV4, you just described -- you just said, "They beat Medunjanin with batons and a cable." Who were you referring to when you said "they"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: I was referring to Zigic and Duca. Both of them beat him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You also said they were carrying batons and a cable. Can you give a better description of the baton and the cable.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: The baton was something like a police baton, whereas the cable, I think it was a black cable -- it was a piece of cable. It was probably plastified, electric cable.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long did this beating go on for approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Well, it went on for about 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you describe the severity or intensity of this beating that you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Well, the blows were very hard. And as I have already said, the -- his head was deformed in a certain sense. And as a result of the blows, blood was gushing out of his neck, I couldn't see any particular cut to the neck. In the end, Medunjanin no longer reacted to the blows, so I assume that he had already lost consciousness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said this was taking place -- have a look at -- outside the room. Are you referring to the corridor area which is marked "A2" on that diagram?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Yes. That was in the corridor where "A2" is marked on the diagram. The door to the room A4 was open, so everything could be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What, if anything, did you hear Mr. Zigic and Duca say to Mr. Medunjanin all during the beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: I don't remember them saying anything to Medunjanin, or rather, I didn't pay any attention. I can't remember right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long were you in the "white house" for on that day, and how did you come to leave the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: We were in the "white house" for about two hours, I think. While he was being beaten, Zigic said we would meet the same fate if we didn't -- look -- or if we were looking. He said we had to face the other side. At the end of that torture, a guard appeared, someone who had been guarding us. He wanted to take us out. While we were passing by - I don't know whether it was Zigic or Duca - but one of them entered the A1 room, and since we were looking in front of us, we then went outside, whereas Medunjanin remained immobile on the ground in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said earlier you saw blood on Mr. Medunjanin. Was there also blood on the floor or in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Yes, there was blood in the corridor on the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Medunjanin again after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: That was the last time I saw Medunjanin. I never saw him after that event in the camp or anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you hear while you were in Omarska that he had died in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: I only heard rumours according to which Medunjanin had disappeared, that he had been taken away. But as to where he had been taken away, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long after you saw him being beaten did you hear that he'd been taken away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: That's something I heard the following day. On that day, we knew nothing, but usually news would be provided by the prisoners in the morning, the news from the previous day and the previous night.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want you to describe Mr. Zigic as you saw him on that day, of course bearing in mind it's been -- it's been 12 years since then. Can you please tell us his approximate height, complexion, build, and age.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: He's over 1 metre and 80 centimetres tall. I don't know his exact height. He has black hair. He's dark-skinned. He had longish hair at the time. He was in a camouflage uniform, not a civilian one but a military uniform. At the time, he was about 35 or 36. That's a rough estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about Duca? Can you give us a description of this person Duca -- or first of all, had you ever -- had you seen Duca before this day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: No. I'd never seen the person called Duca before. He wasn't as tall as Zigic. He had fair hair. He was well built; he was a little plump, that's what I mean. At the time, he was very red in the face. I don't know whether this was because of the heat or because he was excited. He was also wearing a camouflage uniform, and he was over 30 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember -- I withdraw that. Have you seen Mr. Zigic or Duca since that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: I can't remember whether I saw them after that day in the camp. After I had left the camp, I didn't see them again.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember an investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor in The Hague showing you some photographs on the 14th of June, 1999 - that's almost seven years after this incident - showing you a series of 12 photographs? Do you remember being shown those photographs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Yes. I remember them showing me some photographs on one occasion. I can't remember how many photographs they showed me. The two or three sheets containing a number of photographs on them. We were asked to say whether we could identify any of the individuals on those photographs. I had -- after I had had a look at the photographs -- after I had had a look at the photographs, there were two that most resembled Zigic, and I decided that it was in fact Zigic. Since quite a long period of time had elapsed and appearances change, it can be difficult to identify people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And when you were looking at the photographs - and you said that there were two that most resembled Zigic - what were you thinking about whether or not you had to choose between one of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Well, I tried to recall the image I had retained from Omarska. And on the basis of the image I had of Zigic from that time, I tried to make a comparison.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: And that's why I made a choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said you made a choice. Did you think in the circumstances you had to make a choice between the two?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the procedure of identifying people should follow certain rules, and the Prosecution is providing instructions to the person identifying individuals. The witness has to follow these rules. I think we have to follow the same procedure. We shouldn't try to avoid those very strict rules that have been in force for a long time in the Tribunal's jurisprudence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, are you objecting to anything in the way counsel has framed this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Of course, Your Honour. I think that such questions should not be allowed, since the witness has been provided with information as to what he should do before he proceeds to identify anyone, and I think that the procedure should be respected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The question is: "Did you think in the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond circumstances you had to make a choice between the two?" Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. I really don't see anything objectionable in that question, so the objection stands overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. KV2, do you remember the question a moment ago? I'm sorry, I called you "KV2". I meant "KV4". The question was: You said you made a choice. Did you think in the circumstances that you had to make a choice between the two photographs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Well, to a certain extent, yes, since I'd been asked to identify someone in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, I would just like to read out one sentence from the warning to the witness. It was read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I really cannot entertain that intervention at this stage. Would you allow counsel to proceed. He has to finish at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. KV4, did you know someone at the time called Dr. Sadikovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I knew him. I knew him before the war, and I also saw him in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was he in the "white house" or on the pista on the day you saw Becir Medunjanin being beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: On that day, I can't remember whether he was in the "white house" but he wasn't on the pista.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And a person called Dalija? D-a-l-i-j-a. And if so, did you see that person in Omarska or in the "white house" on that day, or in the vicinity on the "white house" on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Dalija -- Mehmedalija or just Dalija?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A person called Dalija.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: I don't know anyone by that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. KV4, my name is Slobodan Stojanovic. I'm a lawyer from Belgrade and I represent the accused Zigic. You said that you knew him as a taxi driver from Prijedor. Can you tell us how long you have known him as a taxi driver.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: From before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Since when exactly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Well, I can't say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: One year, eleven years? For how many years?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Two or three years, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that just before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Well, before the war, I'd known him for about three years.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact that during that time Zigic lived or was living in Pula, in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: I don't know where Zigic was living, but Zigic was known to be -- was known as a taxi driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But you said that you had known him for two or three years before the war.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: That doesn't mean that he never came to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could he have worked as a taxi driver if he was living in a place that was over 500 kilometres from Prijedor, in another republic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: They called him a taxi driver, regardless of whether he worked as a taxi driver or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see his taxi vehicle? Did you ever see him driving a taxi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: I know him as Zigic, the taxi driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You heard such things about him, but I want to know what direct knowledge you have about him. Did you ever see him driving a taxi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: No, I never saw him working as a taxi driver, but I knew that other people called him Zigic, the taxi driver, but I'd never been in a taxi with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see him working as a taxi driver, driving a taxi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: I saw him at places where taxi drivers can usually be found, where taxi drivers usually wait, but I never saw him in a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Since you heard that he was a taxi driver, did you hear what sort of a taxi he had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: I don't know much about cars, so I couldn't tell you anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My colleague from the Prosecution asked you about identifying Zigic on the photo board from -- we will provide this Trial Chamber [sic] with that document. Would it be correct to say that you pointed to someone who least resembled Zigic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember now. I can't remember whom I chose, because that was over five years ago, so I don't remember the person I pointed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We heard about the period of time you spent in Omarska. Did you hear about someone called Milojica Kos, who was in Omarska? As a guard.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Yes. He was the head of a shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you often see him in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And you didn't recognise him on -- in the photograph either. You pointed to someone else; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Sir, I wasn't told whom I had identified and whom I hadn't -- whom I had identified correctly or not. I just had to point to certain individuals. That was all. I don't know exactly whom I chose.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you went to the "white house" on that day, you saw the room A3 and you saw some people lying on the ground or sitting down. Apart from Becir and Sadeta, can you remember anyone else being there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: I only passed by the door, and I didn't have much time. I saw Sadeta because she was sitting right by the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see her later on when you were leaving -- and this is what it says in your statement that you gave to the Prosecution earlier on. Perhaps you didn't hear the question. I'll repeat it. Did you see Mrs. Sadeta --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: You didn't finish your question. I was waiting for you to finish the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, but that was the question. When you left the "white house" - and I think that this is what you stated in the statement - did you see her before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Yes, she remained in the room. I didn't look, but I didn't see them taking her out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what Sadeta looked like at the time, what sort of clothes was she wearing? You said that you knew her better than Becir himself. Was she in uniform, in civilian clothing? What was the colour of her clothes? Is there anything you know about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: She was thin. She had fair hair. She was wearing some sort of a shirt. She didn't have a jacket. She wasn't in uniform. She was extremely thin.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the clothes Becir Medunjanin was wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: He had a shirt on, a dark shirt. I don't remember the colour. And he was wearing trousers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was he wearing dark trousers too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, did you see Becir and Sadeta's son in the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Since I didn't know Medunjanin's children, even if I had seen him, I wouldn't have known that it was his son.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone tell you anything about his son? They spoke to you about Medunjanin himself. Did anyone tell you anything about his son?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: I only heard that one of their sons was with him. That's all I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And next to Medunjanin, did you notice a young man while Medunjanin was being beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: He couldn't be, as Medunjanin was in the corridor and the other prisoners remained in room A3.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So Medunjanin was the only one of the prisoners in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In connection with Zigic, you said that he was wearing a camouflage military uniform. What colour was it? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: When one says "camouflage," I can't really remember whether it was olive-grey/green or was it multicoloured. I just know that it was a military uniform and not civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that apply to the trousers as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How was Zigic beating Medunjanin? We heard you mention a baton, et cetera. Was he holding that baton in his hand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Well, where else, if he was beating with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you see both his hands?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: I didn't really look carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But if you saw the baton, then I assume you must have been able to see what he was holding the baton with.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Well, he was holding it in his hand. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was Zigic wearing any kind of cap?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: I think that he didn't have anything on his head. As I remember well his thick black hair, so I don't think he was wearing a hat.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he have any bandages on him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Especially a bandage on his hand.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: I don't remember, really I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: There are two possible answers. One is "I don't remember." For Zigic and Duca, you said that you don't remember that you saw them in Omarska but you're quite sure that you didn't see them once you left Omarska. So could you explain that a little. It seems rather vague. First a vague answer and then a very explicit answer. So I would have thought that they meant much more to you while you were in Omarska, in the negative sense, than afterwards.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Sir, you must know that in Omarska there was a special kind of psychosis that prevailed, and I couldn't look closely at the guards and know who was present and who was not. But I was explicit in my second part of the answer because when I left the camp, I was virtually under house arrest, as I didn't go into town because I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I just wanted the -- to clarify the first part of your answer. Because when you say "I don't remember seeing them" could mean that you may have seen them but you don't remember that. So did you see them in Omarska or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: If you want an explicit answer, I did not see them after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And before this incident, had you seen them in Omarska, any one of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: No, I had not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How well were you able to see this event, as you were in a room that is in a sense around the corner? So were you able to see this event in each and every detail?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: In view of the fact that I was close to the door, I could observe well what was happening in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there anyone between you and the door?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So you were the first person, closest to the door.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of a person called Fadil Avdagic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of a person called Mesinovic Sabahudin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of a person called Mesinovic Ibrahim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Are you -- do you mean Mesinovic or Mesanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mesinovic, the same surname of Sabahudin.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of a person called Senad Ferhatovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of a person called Abdulah Brkic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was he with you on that occasion in the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of a person called Azedin Oklopcic, a young teacher?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was he in the "white house" on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of a person called Faruk Hrncic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Hrncic Faruk?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Hrncic Faruk.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: I did know a person called Hrncic. Now, whether his first name was Faruk or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of a person called Vahid Besic, known as Vajta?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was he in the "white house" as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of a person called Uzeir Balic from Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I am not mistaken, you testified in the court in Sanski Most in connection with the death of certain individuals in Omarska before Judge Ridesic Emina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Yes. But I don't know which case you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that doesn't really matter. But, for example, Trta Emir Mekinovic and so on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you testify about their death on the basis of any firm knowledge you may have had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: I never said that -- anything but that they had disappeared from the camp. That's all I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg Your Honours for your indulgence for a few more seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You witnessed the beating, as you said, but you didn't hear any shouts or yelling by Zigic and Duca, what they said to Becir and what he answered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: This was not happening in the corridor, so it was in the room. If there was any shouting, it was inside. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So while they were beating him in the corridor, they didn't say anything nor did he say anything in reply.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of a person called Ibrahim Osmancevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that in your written statement to the OTP earlier on you said that when Becir was brought to the corridor, his face only had bruises and no blood, and then the beating continued, and later on you said that blood was gushing from his neck. So my question is: Is it true that when he was brought to the corridor, there was no blood on his face?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: I never said categorically that there was no blood on his face. I said that there were bruises on the face. But now, whether there was blood, that seems to be a fine point. I can't remember now whether there was blood and bruises.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, anyway, it is paragraph 6 of your statement given a few months ago, that is, the 25th of February, 2004. You say, "I was about three metres away from Becir and I saw traces of the beating on his face because it was covered in bruises, but it was not bloodied." Do you remember saying that now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: I may have said that, if that is what it says, but I can't be quite sure whether there was blood or not. I just remember the image of his face covered with bruises.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice anything in connection with his nose?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: A very specific question: Was his nose all cut up? Did you notice that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: I did not, since I couldn't look for any length of time at his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank the witness. I thank Your Honours. I have no further questions. We should like to tender into evidence the witness's statement dated the 25th of February, 2004 and a document on the identification which we received as a courtesy from our learned friends from the Prosecution on a document -- of a document on the identification of Zoran Zigic by the investigator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Well, this second document to which you refer came to you from your colleague on the opposite side. You're proposing to tender that document through this witness. Have you laid the foundation for it? Have you asked this witness whether he was given any guidelines at the time, and if so, whether these were the guidelines?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this was already referred to by questions from my learned friend from the Prosecution and through my objections, but I think that yesterday we admitted into evidence two identical documents -- or rather, documents of the same kind, and I did ask a few questions, but without repeating anything that has already been said. So maybe there's very little left for me to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, if I can help you. Mr. Re, do you have any objections to that document being tendered?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Oh, well, then you may. Now, I will call upon Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions from us either, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Is there any re-examination? By Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. There are two specific points.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. KV4, in response to questions from Mr. Stojanovic, you referred to a kind of psychosis that prevailed from Omarska and I couldn't look closely at the guards." What did you mean by "a special kind of psychosis"? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: What I meant was, with reference to the time we spent on the pista, so as not to see who was passing by and who they were bringing in for interrogation, in most cases we were lying face down without turning our heads left or right, and we were not allowed to look around or even at the guards. That is the psychosis of fear, fear of not being noticed looking and seeing what you were not supposed to see, as you could suffer consequences otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were those consequences?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: There would be beating. The guard -- the guard would call out a prisoner and beat him. That is what would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic also asked you about your recognition of Mr. Zigic when you saw him in the "white house" and questioned you about your recognition of him -- or your knowledge of him before Omarska. Now -- again, we all appreciate it's been a very long time, 12 years, but can you tell us approximately how many times you would have seen him around Prijedor before Omarska.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: It is very hard for me to give you an answer now, but I assume three or four times at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And how did you come to know that he was Zigic, the taxi driver? Were there any other places you saw him, apart from in the taxi area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: I saw him once in a bar, and other people told me, "That is Zigic," and it is from then on that I knew who Zigic, the taxi driver was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May I ask one little question: Witness, you spoke of Mr. Zigic, the taxi driver. I take it you were familiar with the town? You had lived in the town for some time? How long had you lived in the town for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Yes. I was born in Prijedor, and I spent my whole working lifetime in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, this taxi stand to which you referred was in the central part of the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: It was at the railway station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The railway station.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: Yes. And there was one next to the hotel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: If there was another taxi driver called Zigic, would you know that? Could you tell from your knowledge of the place whether there was another taxi driver by the name of Zigic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: If there had been another taxi driver with the same name, I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KV4
utterances.text: But I think that such a person did not exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And such a person did not exist; I see. Thank you. Thank you very much. [Microphone not activated] I think we have come to the end of this part -- oh, the microphone. We can ask the witness now to stand down, and we will take a break of 30 minutes and then we will come back to hear the conclusions of the parties on the evidence which has been led. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. The sitting is resumed. Mr. Stojanovic or Mr. Zigic. Ready, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Yes, I am ready. But there is something I would like to say. I wouldn't want to have this -- these proceedings prolonged, but rebuttal witnesses have provided so many falsehoods, so many inconsistencies, and this was especially the case in the case of witnesses who support the judgement. I could in fact write about 200 pages about all the falsehoods they have presented. I think a far better solution would be to give us a deadline so that we could provide you with certain written submissions about all these matters. I could state my position today and provide certain explanations about certain key issues, certain matters that we have heard about in the course of these three days, but I think that there are too many issues to be addressed in 30 minutes, especially after just a half an hour break. With regard to the last witness, I think I could write about 50 pages on all the falsehoods presented. I think that these falsehoods would be catastrophic, not only for the additional witnesses of the Defence but also with regard to the witnesses on the basis of which the judgement is based. This has to do with the Witness T and Fadil Avdagic. What the rebuttal witnesses said is in contradiction with over 90 per cent of what was said by Witness T and Fadil Avdagic, and the judgement is based on these witnesses. It's less in contradiction with the witnesses who were favourable to the Defence. But we would first of all like to remind the Trial Chamber that in our response to the Prosecution, pursuant to Rule 115, we expressed our position and stated that the reasons for the appeal are sufficient to change many things contained in the judgement, especially with regard to the murder of Drago Tokmadzic and Becir Medunjanin. The additional evidence is in fact superfluous, in our opinion, but our opinion is probably not going to be accepted by each individual Judge. With regard to these two murders, the murder of Becir Medunjanin and Drago Tokmadzic, we expressed our position in a grotesque -- with a slightly grotesque example concerning the additional evidence. There is nothing decisive about this evidence, in our opinion; although this is something that is requested according to Rule 115. Even before additional evidence was presented, as we have already said, there was far more evidence that supported the idea that there was nothing to prove these two murders. If we now add certain weight to these matters, well, in fact there is really nothing decisive to prove the case. We must point out that over the last three days -- the Defence hasn't forgotten about this matter -- but the additional evidence doesn't only relate to the murder of Becir Medunjanin but also to the torture of Witness T. According to the judgement, these two acts are inseparable, are completely inseparable. Becir Medunjanin and Witness T were beaten at the same time. Those who beat them, allegedly Zigic and Duca, took turns to do so, and they beat them one next to the other. So each witness who claims that he only saw Medunjanin being beaten or claims that he only saw Witness T being beaten is in fact stating something that is contrary to the judgement, because this is inseparable according to the judgement. The only difference is that Becir Medunjanin succumbed to his wounds, whereas Witness T survived the beating. They were only half a metre or a metre from each other when they were beaten, and people took turns to beat them. We've also heard from the rebuttal witness that no one touched Witness T and that no one saw him, and Witness T was a key witness here, and he spoke about the terrible experience that he and Becir Medunjanin had been through. I just want to say that the Defence has been faced with a very difficult test, given that through -- it had four witnesses provided for additional evidence. They were Prosecution -- this was Prosecution evidence, in fact, whereas the Defence witnesses that we suggested - there were about 30 of them - and none of them were accepted. We heard four witnesses which were in fact Prosecution witnesses. They were witnesses for the other side. And the consequence of this conflict that we are talking about can still be felt, and we can see this as a result of the subpoena and protective measures. This is something that also appears in their written statements. In any event, we had four hostile witnesses. That's what the Anglo-Saxon term would be. Two of them were allegedly for our benefit. But we didn't object to that, because we wanted to show the Chamber that we weren't afraid of the truth, not in the least, and we wanted to add additional weight to our appeal. And we do request that the Trial Chamber bear this fact in mind. With regard to the evidence that we obtained through KV1 in March, we stated at the time what our position was, and I don't think that this is an issue that needs to be addressed today. We heard Witness KV2. The witness was obviously under the influence of the Prosecution. It's not a matter of pressure exerted by the Prosecution, but circumstances were such. Australia is Mr. Blewitt's country, Staker's country, Mr. Re's country, and I assume that the Prosecution either directly or through the Victims and Witnesses Unit helped most of them to find a home in Australia. I was personally able to become persuaded of this fact, to see this fact. With regard to victims of Serbian nationality --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Stojanovic, I'm not sure how I should understand your references to Australia. Are you making a proposition you would like to present to us for consideration?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I didn't want to accuse anyone, and I didn't have anything negative in mind. In the following few sentences, you will hear what the point I want to make is. I've personally been able to see that in the case of Serbian witnesses, in the case of the Celebici camp, when I cooperated or worked with the Prosecution, many victims of Serbian nationality were taken there. They are grateful to the Prosecution, and they wouldn't want to Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond be a party that is opposed to them. This is just a humane gesture. I'd like the Chamber to bear this in mind. They wouldn't want to support the opposing side and they wouldn't want to disappoint the Prosecution. KV2 had more contact with the Prosecution, as a future witness for the Prosecution. This witness gave a number of statements, but they never heard -- they never had any contact with the Defence. So the fact that he could be influenced is quite understandable, and the Prosecution did put very leading questions to this witness. But what is really obvious in the case of this witness, in the first and in the second written statement as well as in this witness's oral testimony, is that Zigic did not participate in the beating and murder of Becir Medunjanin, not in any way. Zigic was a person who was excluded from this event. On the other hand, the other side tried to minimise the importance of certain issues by asking whether it was possible for someone to enter the "white house" without being noticed and join those who were committing crimes there. It's quite possible. I could also ask whether it's possible for an earthquake to occur now, and everyone will say, "Yes, it's possible." But that is not the point. We're not talking about secondary individuals who may have entered the facility after they had started committing the act. We're talking about the person who was the initiator. Someone might enter the courtroom now, but I'm sure that it won't be the President of the Chamber or one of the Judges. It wouldn't be possible not to notice this. So we're talking about the key individuals after the act had already been initiated. If someone subsequently entered the premises, this could only be someone who joined them. But it could not be Zigic. And this is what results from the statements of witnesses that we received in the course of the trial. As far as the rebuttal witnesses are concerned, I could state a few things for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, but I would like to ask the Trial Chamber to give me the possibility of doing this in writing. I think that the testimony is catastrophic in relation to the judgement and the sentence handed down to Zigic by the Trial Chamber, naturally, if the alleged facts are taken to be true. This testimony is in contradiction to the statements of Witness T and of witness Fadil Avdagic. In addition to other shortcomings, naturally the main shortcoming is the fact that it is impossible to identify the individual. In our appeal, we complained about the standards applied by this Trial Chamber in the Kupreskic case. We think that far less was required there than is required in this case. In that case, it had to do with the identification of one witness, but here we have the identification provided by one witness but we mustn't forget that we have eight witnesses who claim the contrary. KV3 more or less admitted yesterday that he mixed Zigic up with someone else. He recognised Zigic on the photo board as someone who sold beer, and as he himself said, as someone who had nothing to do with the murder of Medunjanin. We would even say that there are two alternatives with respect to this witness: Either the witness saw nothing in the "white house," or we need to trust everything he says. Both options are favourable for Zigic. Even the latter could be said to be more favourable, in which he says that the person selling beer was Zigic, and he actually confused the two and he said that he was not involved in the killing of Medunjanin. However, we have expressed serious doubts that he was present there at all. He said with respect to Witness T that he wasn't beaten up there. Let us read through once again what Witness T says. He's mentioned at least 10 to 15 times in the judgement, and the guilty sentence is based on his statement. He says that he was wearing a blue uniform, and we have heard from at least 30 witnesses that he was wearing a green uniform. Fadil Avdagic tells us that he had black trousers. Today's witness told us that he had camouflage trousers. The description of Duca, we hear for the first time that Duca was fair, blond. I think that the Court has had occasion to see what he looks like. He's small, quite plump. He's here in the Detention Unit and his hair is not fair, so this is a notorious fact for the Court, notoria non probatur, one might say. One person says that he was fair with short hair; the other that he was fair with long hair. But Witness T said that he was dark. Both witnesses mention Sadeta Medunjanin. They describe her with confidence. She was present there, they say. What does Witness T tell us? The next day - I won't now indicate the relationship - Sadeta Medunjanin was taken from the "white house" and put up with the other women; transcript 2567. On that same page of the transcript, the same is repeated. For instance, 2658 gives a detailed description of her leaving the building two days prior to the murder of Becir. We are told how Zeljko Meakic took her out to the administrative building to join the other witnesses. And then there are details about Witness T meeting Sadeta and informing her of the death of Becir Medunjanin. So both witnesses clearly made up this fact, but they did it well, this fabrication. How can we explain their continued statements with respect to the description of that woman? Unfortunately -- I'm always trying to act in good faith, but in this case I cannot be positive. Some say she had a shirt, a long skirt, light hair. We have heard a detailed description of that woman by the rebuttal witness, and the Judges are aware of the relationships between Witness T and that woman and how much he might have known about that lady, and I think that we have to believe him because otherwise the judgement does not stand. So with respect to Sadeta, the rebuttal witnesses are intentionally not telling the truth. It is not a question of a mistake. One of them said that there were no other women in the "white house." Not a single of these witnesses noticed bandages on Zigic's hands. We insisted on this point. I don't know to what extent Your Honours are aware of that. The Trial Chamber was. About two weeks prior to this event the forefinger of Zigic's left hand was cut off. He can show you that now. A shell cut off this finger, and his whole left hand had a very large bandage around it. Therefore, the statement of one of the witnesses that he wore fingerless gloves is quite impossible without -- and it is also impossible that no one noticed those bandages. And with respect to those bandages at the time, we have innumerable pieces of evidence to support it. We have the testimony of the expert witness, Mirko Barudzija, Exhibit KVD/24, I think. Many witnesses, all the Defence witnesses, and at least 10 to 15 Prosecution witnesses mentioned as an important identification factor the large bandages round his left hand. Several days after this incident, he was again subjected to surgery. He spent seven days in hospital because the wound became infected, so obviously they didn't recognise Zigic. Today's witness -- Your Honours, you will have occasion to see that photograph because instead of Zigic he pointed to someone else, a person who doesn't at all resemble Zigic, a completely different face. And he also said that the person next to this one was Kos, which was again wrong. So he was wrong twice. Trying to tell us that he knew Zigic as a taxi driver is hearsay evidence, because we hear that he never met him. He heard that about him from others. A taxi driver before the war, he says; and when I told him that Zigic was not living there before the war, then he said he might have travelled from Pula to act as a taxi driver. This is not an error; it is an ill-intentioned statement, for someone to come from another state to act as a taxi driver along rather bad roads is hardly credible. Today's witness also never heard of a long list of names that I mentioned to him and of whom we know that were present in the "white house." He never heard of any one of them, except Abdulah Brkic, but that's fine. Abdulah Brkic is a taxi driver who knows Zigic very well; however, he testified against him and said that he had testified in certain incidents. But with respect to Becir Medunjanin he was explicit. He said, "Zigic has nothing to do with this murder. He did not participate in the killing nor in the beating up of Witness T." This witness, as opposed to maybe up to 20 others, is the only one who never heard of Dalija, Dalija Hrnic, as opposed to all the other witnesses. Both rebuttal witnesses said, if I'm not mistaken, that they never saw Zigic and Duca before or after the incident in Omarska, and the judgement says that Zigic regularly entered the camp. One of the characteristics noted by all the witnesses of this incident and confirmed by Witness T is that Duca had previously cut a nostril of Becir Medunjanin's even before coming to the "white house" and that that is why the nostril was bleeding profusely. This witness didn't see that. My client told me -- in connection with this last statement that there was no other Zigic in Prijedor, my client tells me that there was. This is something I hear for the first time. But I don't wish to prolong this endlessly because I have a deadline for any new submissions under Rule 115. Anyway, this witness did not provide evidence of death but of Becir Medunjanin's unconsciousness. I do believe that I have left out at least half of the omissions made by these two rebuttal witnesses. You may not be surprised if I make up for it in writing, regardless of whether that will be admitted or not for formal reasons, but I am always a supporter of the view that the Appeals Chamber has great discretionary powers with respect to the procedure and determination as to whether they will admit anything or not. So this is exclusively in your hands, Your Honours. utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the Bench has considered your proposal to submit written arguments, and the Bench is of the view that the application should be refused. utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The test is very, very clearly set out in Rule 115 and Rule 117(A) as to what the Appeals Chamber has to do. The test is: Has the appellant established that no reasonable tribunal of fact could have reached a conclusion of guilt based upon the evidence before the Trial Chamber together with additional evidence admitted during the appellant proceedings? And this, of course, includes the rebuttal evidence which the Prosecution has led. And considering the evidence, the Appeals Chamber is, of course, guided by Rule 117, which provides the appellant -- sorry. "The Appeals Chamber shall pronounce judgement on the basis of the record on appeal together with such additional evidence as has been presented to it." And of course, I refer Your Honours, as you of course well know, to the Kupreskic appeals judgement at pages 75 -- sorry, paragraphs 75 and 76. So what is the state of the case now, having heard the additional evidence brought on behalf, or at the request of the appellant Mr. Zigic and the rebuttal evidence brought by the Prosecution? The Prosecution's -- the Respondent's submission in one line is that it has strengthened the case which was -- which could have been before the Trial Chamber, and had the Trial Chamber had the benefit of both the rebuttal and the additional evidence, it could have made findings -- it could have -- it could have added to its findings. It could have strengthened its findings in relation to the finding against the appellant Mr. Zigic. Of course in these sorts of circumstances one will never get an entirely consistent account. You bear in mind the circumstances. You have what is basically a concentration camp, people confined in the most horrific conditions, not knowing whether they will live from one day to another, not knowing whether they are the next person whose name is going to be put on a list and called out never to be seen again. You've got people who see some things and people who see other things. You get people in a situation where there are many people coming and going, and in circumstances of extreme fear one can never expect the same version from the various people who witnessed either the whole incidents or various parts of the events. And were you to do so, you would be entitled to be suspicious of it, because in these circumstances people never remember things in the same manner. And this is particularly acute when you're considering that the witnesses at trial were giving evidence eight years after the event and the additional witness, KV2 and KV3 and KV4 on the last two days, the rebuttal witnesses, are doing so 12 years after the event. The normal psychological processes which play in a person's mind are people try to forget these sorts of things. People forget the little details. People forget who was there and the order of things. But - and this is the important part, when you bear in mind the Trial Chamber -- the evidence before the Trial Chamber, its findings, the additional evidence and the rebuttal evidence - is the common thread running through the evidence at trial, the additional evidence, and the rebuttal evidence. And these, in the Prosecution's submissions, are the things that witnesses remember. Witnesses remember the most important things. The threads which are running through here, in what the -- in this case -- and Your Honours, this case is not an identification case; it's a recognition case. The additional evidence -- had it been before the Trial Chamber, the Trial Chamber would have had a better view of the recognition of Mr. Zigic at the time as a person the two additional witnesses KV3 and KV4 recognised as Zigic, the taxi driver from Prijedor, rather than identified either in court or from photo boards or many, many years later. These are the threads running through the case: People recognised Mr. Zigic as a taxi driver from Prijedor, although Witness T didn't; Witness T was told at the time by someone who did know Mr. Zigic as a taxi driver from Prijedor. That's one thread. Another thread is that there was a beating of Becir Medunjanin, and the witnesses all knew who Becir Medunjanin, who was a reasonably prominent person in the community in the area, they knew who he was. The next thread is that this beating -- particular beating occurred in the "white house" in Omarska. The next one is that it was in approximately mid-June 1992, when all of the witnesses were there. Another thread is that there were a lot of people in the "white house" at the time, a lot of different people. Another thread is that Mr. Medunjanin was beaten severely and suffered severe injuries. And the final thread which runs through the additional evidence of each of the witnesses heard at trial, the additional evidence and the rebuttal evidence is that Mr. Medunjanin died, was never seen again afterwards. And the only inference available from that, when combined with T's evidence, is that he died as a result of these particularly severe beatings. The two additional witnesses, KV3 and KV4, have also described a baton which Mr. Zigic and Duca had with them. This is, of course, referred to in the judgement, the evidence of Witness T, as Mr. Zigic having a special kind of baton. And you heard KV3 yesterday describe a spring-type of baton. This is one of the things, you would expect, witnesses may recall. It's one of the smaller details, something that may stand out. The Defence has -- Mr. Stojanovic, in cross-examination of the additional -- two additional witnesses, cross-examined them as to their "identification" or lack of, or failure to identify Mr. Zigic, if you could put it that way, from a photo board many years later. Now, I think one of the witnesses, Mr. Avdagic, summed this up very well when he was asked at trial if he could recognise or identify Mr. Zigic in court, and of course there are many problems, as the Appeals Chamber is aware, of courtroom identification, and especially so long after the event. This appears at page 3.444 of the transcript, in which the Prosecutor asked Mr. Avdagic: "Mr. Avdagic, I know that eight years have passed since that time, but do you think that you could recognise Zoran Zigic today?" To which Mr. Avdagic gave the most honest and sensible reply that anyone in his position could: "I cannot claim that with certainty. We have all changed a lot." And that was on the 4th of July, 2000. Yet he was able to recognise Mr. Zigic from the four -- the four people -- the people in court at the time -- the five in court at the time. But what we have here is two witnesses, KV3 and KV4, being shown photographs, firstly in 1999 and then in 2000, respectively eight and nine years -- I'm sorry, seven and eight years after the events -- after they witnessed this most horrific beating, during which time they hadn't seen Mr. Zigic or Duca. The description they both gave matches the general description of the person they recognised contemporaneously as Zigic and, of course, recognised what the Appeals Chamber -- recognised what the Appeals Chamber can see is a reasonably good description of Mr. Zigic. If I could specifically turn to Exhibit DA2 on appeal, that is, the photo board which was shown to Witness KV3 and which was tendered yesterday. The exhibit -- and this was something Mr. Stojanovic made something of in his submissions. When shown photographs, the witness said, "I recognise this person from the camp. He came in a pick-up truck." The photograph, of course, which he was talking of was in fact Mr. Zigic. Now, in those circumstances, some eight years later, it is not a reliable form of identification. But you have to bear in mind that he has recognised a person on that page who is indeed Mr. Zigic, and in that respect, when you put that together with the circumstances of identification, he is clearly recognising someone who was there at the time. The second one is DA5, which was the photo board shown to today's witness, Mr -- Witness KV4.
